articles.title: A day after Wangchuk compares Ladakh situation with Tibet; Central Tibetan Administration calls comparison misplaced, inaccurate
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: A day after Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk compared situation in Ladakh with Tibet, the Central Tibetan
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A day after Leh Apex Body (LAB) member and climate activist Sonam Wangchuk compared situation in Ladakh with Tibet, the Central Tibetan Administration, based in Dharamshala, Friday evening expressed deep concern over remarks of Wangchuk called the comparison misplaced and inaccurate and stating “Tibet continues to remain under China's authoritarian rule.”“The Central Tibetan Administration expresses deep concern over remarks made by Sonam Wangchuk in his recent public speech in Ladakh, in which he compared the situation in Ladakh with that of inside Tibet,” Tenzin Lekshay official spokesperson of the Central Tibetan Administration said, adding that CTA considers such a comparison misplaced and inaccurate.“His statement doesn't reflect the real situation inside Tibet. Tibet continues to remain under China's authoritarian rule. where Tibetans face systematic repression of their fundamental rights, religious freedom; and intensification of measures aimed at erasing its distinct cultural identity,” Lekshay added.Wangchuk, addressing people in Leh on the first anniversary of the Sept 24, 2025 violence, said the alleged breach of promises made to Ladakh over the Sixth Schedule and statehood was the “root cause” of last year’s protests.On September 24 2025, police allegedly opened fire on protesters demanding Sixth Schedule status and statehood for Ladakh after demonstrations turned violent, killing four people and injuring nearly 90.He feared he could be subjected to an “encounter” for speaking out against what he called atrocities in Ladakh, a year after police firing killed four protesters in Leh. Drawing a comparison with Tibet, Wangchuk said Ladakhis had chosen India because of its democracy.“Today, such atrocities are being committed in Ladakh that even China is not doing in Tibet. That is what you are seeing today,” he said.He sought a people’s tribunal to probe the killings, saying a judicial commission set up by Union home ministry had yet to submit its report. “Last year on this day, four people died... Bullets hit their chests, backs, and heads. Those were not pellets that would merely injure you or hurt your eyes. Bullets were fired indiscriminately from automatic weapons, like AK-47s, at the unarmed youth of Ladakh who were peacefully demanding their rights,” Wangchuk alleged. He rejected claims that the protests were triggered by him. He alleged that before the 2020 LAHDC-Leh elections, Ladakhi representatives opposed to holding polls were taken to New Delhi on a special flight and promised statehood and Sixth Schedule status.He blamed “govt failure to honour those promises” for last year’s demonstrations. Authorities imposed curfew-like restrictions in Leh after the alleged “arson and rioting” and subsequent police firing last year. FIRs were filed and 81 people arrested, including Wangchuk. He was charged under NSA and sent to Jodhpur jail. After 170 days, Union govt withdrew his detention on March 14 this year and he was set free.He feared further action, saying: “They sent me to jail. Inquiries have been made against me. Only an encounter is left. I am ready for that. It is my last wish. Experts tell me that you will be subjected to an encounter. So be it. Let the country wake up, this is my hope.”A complete shutdown was observed in Leh on Thursday, designated as Martyr’s Day. Wangchuk accused authorities of stopping people from attending the rally, a claim denied by police.Police said the Ladakh Buddhist Association had sought permission for a public meeting at Leh’s NDS stadium, which has a capacity of 10,000. The administration granted permission for a prayer meet from 10am to noon. articles.title: Why Russia is sending dead princes and saints into battle
articles.summary: As Russian troops on the front lines of eastern Ukraine are digging in for another winter, they are receiving an unusual form of support.
articles.body: As Russian troops on the front lines of eastern Ukraine are digging in for another winter, they are receiving an unusual form of support: the remains of a warrior prince who fought for Moscow more than six centuries ago. A fragment of the remains of Dmitry Donskoy, a prince celebrated in Russia for his victory at the Battle of Kulikovo in 1380, was sent to the front lines in early September and is now being sent around military bases in Russian-occupied Ukraine. The military department of the Moscow Patriarchate, the Russian Orthodox Church’s clerical leadership, said the “saint commander” would invisibly stand “shoulder to shoulder” with Russian soldiers. The church added that the relic, a fragment of his right hand, was the same hand with which he wielded his sword at Kulikovo. Sending a religious relic into battle may seem peculiar but since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow has sought to use every avenue in what has become a grinding and bloody war of attrition, including invoking religious symbolism to portray its cause as “righteous” and divinely sanctioned. As a result, the relationship between the Kremlin and the Russian Orthodox Church has grown closer than ever. “The church has practically merged with the state to the point of being indistinguishable,” said Sergei Chapnin, a religious scholar and director of communications at Fordham University’s Orthodox Christian Studies Center. “From my point of view, the maximum (closeness) has been reached.” ‘A mobilizing myth’ Dispatching sacred relics to troops is a longstanding practice in Orthodox Christianity. “This combination of the sacred and the material attracts attention,” said Chapnin, who used to work in the publishing house of the Moscow Patriarchate. “Of course, propaganda uses this.” The remains of Donskoy also carry a contemporary message, experts say. “He was not himself an aggressor, but a defender of the fatherland,” the scholar told CNN. From the government’s perspective, “it is very important to show that Russia is not the aggressor, that we are defending our territory.” Chapnin called it “a mobilizing myth.” “These myths, which connect different times and eras, can act quite powerfully on mass consciousness,” he said, adding that the relics are presented as “a magical artifact.” Metropolitan Vladimir, the Russian-installed Orthodox leader in Donetsk and Mariupol, said the relic would help soldiers and civilians “mobilize both their spiritual and physical strength” and “triumph over the enemy.” Donskoy is not the first warrior saint Russia has invoked during its war in Ukraine. Relics of Prince Alexander Nevsky, another medieval ruler-turned-symbol of Russian military glory, were also taken to troops earlier this year. The timing of sending Donskoy’s remains into battle was also handy. The prince’s remains were uncovered during restoration work at the Kremlin’s Archangel Cathedral in August, weeks after unverified reports that the Nevsky relics had been lost. Russian President Vladimir Putin called the recovery of the remains – whose location had been known since their burial – an “absolutely unique” and “marvelous discovery.” The pro-Kremlin leader of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, described it as “a special sign of God’s providence. But for the Rev. Alexander Zanemonets, an Orthodox priest and historian born in Moscow who lived abroad for years before leaving Russia permanently after its invasion of Ukraine, the discovery “has nothing to do with Christianity.” “It is undoubtedly the exploitation of Christianity and the exploitation of the church for ‘patriotic’ purposes.” In a church with relatively few active worshippers but strong state backing, incentives tend to align with the state, he said, calling the use of the remains a “cynical calculation.” From 2022 to 2024, Zanemonets ministered to Ukrainian war refugees in the Orthodox Church of Finland. His service ended amid questions about his Ukrainian-language proficiency and ties to Russia, allegations he rejected in a Facebook post. ‘We are Russians. God is with us.’ While it may appear cynical to some, many of those at the front have found themselves turning to God. “Not all of us talk to God when things are going well, but everyone talks to God when things are bad,” one former Russian serviceman who previously fought in Ukraine told CNN. He described makeshift churches built from whatever was available, soldiers praying before every mission and priests regularly visiting military units and hospitals. “Like a field kitchen, there should be a priest everywhere,” he said, quoting a popular Russian expression: “We are Russians. God is with us.” A Russian soldier currently serving in the Zaporizhzhia region also described the opportunity to speak to a priest, pray or touch a holy object as “serious moral support.” As the war drags into its fifth year with no end in sight, the troops say the strain is growing. “The situation is tense overall and is only getting worse as the time goes on,” a Russian commander in Donbas told CNN. The soldiers discussed their faith at the front on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. Away from the front lines, the Russian Orthodox Church’s religious reach appears far more limited than its demonstrated political influence. A 2026 telephone survey by the state-run pollster VСIOM found about two-thirds of Russians identify as Orthodox Christians, down from roughly 80% 15 years ago. But several priests and religious scholars told CNN that only about 2% of baptized Orthodox believers in Russia regularly practice their faith, a figure supported by Russian Interior Ministry data on attendance at Orthodox Christmas services. Yet an annual religious procession promoted by far-right and nationalist groups in four Russian cities drew huge crowds in September, with more than 100,000 participants in Moscow alone, according to official figures. In the capital, worshippers carried a fragment of Donskoy’s relics through the streets in a procession led by Kirill. According to Zanemonets, who now works at the Orthodox Church in America, such events primarily serve to demonstrate to the state how the church “can organize large numbers of people.” Still, religious scholar and historian Konstantin Mikhailov called the turnout “a drop in the ocean” in a country of more than 145 million people, arguing that Russian society, contrary to the wishes of the state and the church, remains very secular. To help expand its own influence, the church receives money and political backing from the Kremlin, while the Kremlin gains legitimacy because the church supports state narratives, Mikhailov argued, calling it a “mutually reinforcing” cycle. ‘How we support them’ The historian also said the cycle has fueled the growth of military chaplains on the front lines. For critics inside the church, however, that raises a difficult question about the kind of assistance priests should offer soldiers. “We need to support people, including those in military uniform,” said the Rev. Grigory Mikhnov-Vaytenko, a Russian priest of the Apostolic Orthodox Church who helps Ukrainian refugees displaced by the war. “But the question is how we support them.” “On the one hand, (you must) not deny people spiritual help, and on the other, not lead them into an illusion,” the priest told CNN. The Russian Orthodox Church has taken a different view. Just days after Putin announced a partial mobilization in September 2022, Patriarch Kirill told worshippers that a soldier who dies while carrying out his military duty has made a sacrifice that “washes away all the sins.” Ukraine has painstakingly sought to break away from the Russian Orthodox Church, formally splitting from it in 2019. Bartholomew I of Constantinople, the head of the global Orthodox church, recognized the establishment of an independent Orthodox Church in Ukraine. Mikhnov-Vaytenko noted that Orthodox Christians make up a majority of the population in both Russia and Ukraine. The priest, who left the Russian Orthodox Church after Moscow’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, said the church as an institution “blesses its children to kill one another.” Fordham University’s Chapnin called it a departure from how martyrdom has been understood in the Orthodox tradition for thousands of years. “The Gospel has a subordinate significance in relation to the tasks of state propaganda,” he said. Meanwhile on the front lines, not every soldier who CNN spoke to saw the relics as meaningful support. One serviceman in the Donbas region, in occupied eastern Ukraine, called it “a very unconventional solution to our problems in the 21st century.” “My view is that they are needed more by the mothers of the guys who died in this military operation,” he added.

articles.title: The US deported LGBTQ migrants to countries where homosexuality makes them a target
articles.summary: Aylin says she fled her home country after her life was threatened. She sought refuge in the US but was deported to a country where her sexuality puts her at risk.
articles.body: “I’m so scared. I want to go outside, because I’m human. But I cannot go outside here.” Aylin, age 28, was sitting in a quiet courtyard in the center of Bangui, the bustling capital of the Central African Republic. She recounted the improbable story that brought her here from her native Turkey – via the United States. She is gay. To protect her from reprisals, CNN is using a pseudonym. Aylin left her home country two years ago. After a religious group and a close family member threatened her life, she said she decided to seek refuge in the United States. “I just hoped to be free. To live my life how I want to live, to take a breath. To have friends. A relationship. A good family. My own family. Justice.” STREAMING NOW: Inside Trump’s secret deportation deals. Upgrade to watch the full report. Soon after arriving in the US, a judge granted Aylin withholding of removal, a form of protection that implies it would be unsafe for her to return to Turkey due to her sexuality. She was denied asylum under a Biden-era border policy that restricted eligibility for many migrants who crossed the southern border outside official pathways. That policy has since been struck down by a federal judge. But in July, after 18 months in US detention, she says she was handcuffed and shackled, then placed on a flight heading for the Central African Republic (CAR). She had never even heard of the country when she learned, mid-flight, that it was their destination. Her case represents a dire example of an already distressing policy, immigration advocates say: The US is deporting scores of people who identify as LGBTQ to countries where that puts them at extreme risk. Living a life in limbo For years, the US offered protection to people who convinced immigration judges that returning home could mean persecution, torture, or death. Now, some of those same people are finding themselves stranded in countries they have never visited, under a rapidly expanding American policy that legal experts say uses a loophole to deport migrants not to their countries of origin, but to third countries willing to receive them. The Trump administration has signed at least 35 agreements with countries across Africa, Latin America and elsewhere, according to the nonprofit initiative Third Country Deportation Watch. Among those caught up in the policy are LGBTQ asylum seekers, like Aylin, who had already won legal protections in US immigration courts. Aylin spent several weeks cooped up in an apartment block in Bangui, the CAR capital, agonizing over her limited options. She was living a life in limbo: rejected by the US, aware that she could not live freely in the country she now found herself – hostility towards homosexuality is widespread in central Africa – and afraid for what might happen if she returned to the very place she’d fled. Despite her fears, she ultimately chose to return to Turkey. “I hope everything has changed for people like me in Turkey,” she told CNN the day before boarding her flight home. “But I’m so scared. Really, I’m so scared.” In recent weeks, Turkey has launched one of its most sweeping crackdowns on LGBTQ rights groups in years. Though homosexuality is legal in Turkey, authorities have carried out coordinated raids targeting LGBTQ advocacy organizations and activists across multiple cities, leading to mass arrests and detentions. Turkish officials have defended September’s operation as part of a campaign to protect traditional family values. ‘Just unconscionable’ Though thousands of migrants have been deported to third countries this year, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, the US government does not provide data on how many of those had sought protection based on characteristics like sexuality. But Bridget Crawford, from Immigration Equality, an NGO that provides legal services for LGBTQ migrants and asylum seekers in the US, believes the numbers have shot up. “It’s terrible for any refugee to be put in that situation, being deported to a country where they have no connections, where they have no support system, where in so many cases, people are being arbitrarily detained where they don’t have a true opportunity for permanent status,” Crawford said. “But if you’re queer or trans and you’re being sent to a country that persecutes queer and trans people, it is just unconscionable.” Human rights groups are especially concerned that nearly half of the countries accepting deportees from the US are African nations, many of which criminalize homosexuality. Reports of a worsening climate for LGBTQ people are rising sharply across parts of the continent, and politicians have increasingly campaigned on anti-LGBTQ platforms. Over several weeks, CNN spoke with several deportees who identify as LGBTQ scattered across Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea and CAR. They all expressed disbelief and terror at being sent to countries where they felt they were now at heightened risk. Adwoa, a 21-year-old bisexual Ghanaian woman, tearfully describes fleeing years of hostility and violence linked to her sexuality when she sought refuge in the US. CNN is also using a pseudonym for her, because of her precarious position. She says her sexuality meant that her neighbors ostracized her family and accused them of witchcraft. But after obtaining a guarantee from a US court that she would not be deported back to Ghana, she was instead sent to Cameroon, where same-sex relations are also illegal, and punishable by up to five years in prison. In fact, Crawford said, her organization has represented several asylum cases for LGBTQ Cameroonian nationals claiming persecution due to their sexuality. “It’s like you’re a criminal,” Adwoa said of her life in Cameroon, where she’s been staying at a government-run detention facility for the last few months. “It’s a terrifying feeling.” She believes she could be killed if she returned to Ghana. Though homosexuality is not illegal in CAR, where Aylin was sent, societal norms mean that maintaining a homosexual relationship is “extraordinarily dangerous,” according to a 2023 report by the US State Department. On the streets of Bangui, CNN encountered open hostility toward LGBTQ people. “We don’t like them. They should be killed,” one person said. Another called for security forces to arrest and punish them. “We don’t want them to live because they are men like us and, since they allow themselves to be penetrated from behind, we don’t like that.” Human rights groups have noted that women in same-sex relationships across Africa can also often face so-called “corrective” sexual violence, assaults, harassment and discrimination. ‘I cannot feel like myself here’ The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has defended its deportation policy, arguing that migrants are receiving due process and that third-country agreements are lawful tools to carry out removal orders. “These third-country agreements, which ensure due process under the U.S. Constitution, are essential to the safety of our homeland and the American people,” DHS said in a statement to CNN. “We are applying the law as written. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.” Critics disagree. “It’s an abdication of both our legal and our moral obligations. Under domestic law, and under international law,” said Crawford. A federal appeals court this month upheld a February ruling that aspects of the administration’s third-country deportation policy were unlawful, raising questions about whether migrants are being given adequate opportunities to challenge transfers to unfamiliar countries. The case is likely headed to the Supreme Court, which has previously allowed deportations to continue by lifting temporary injunctions. For those living in this reality, the political debate feels far away. Aylin is now back in Turkey, where she has told her family that she’s changed her sexual orientation. But she is very far from the freedoms she dreamed of when she left for the US. “I will find a job, I will get money, I will leave secretly for Europe or somewhere else,” she said. “I cannot feel like myself here.”
